title: Providence (CCC 302–308)
hook: God guides creation, and invites us to cooperate

segments.voice: Yesterday, almighty: a power the Catechism says shows most in mercy. Your line was power as mercy. Today, how that power guides.

"Behold the birds of the air, for they neither sow, nor do they reap, nor gather into barns: and your heavenly Father feedeth them." Jesus says it on a hillside, in the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims. It's a lovely line. It also raises a fair question from anyone with a job and a rent payment due on the first. So should we stop sowing? Today's word is the Catechism's way of fitting God's care and our work together: providence.
screen: `THE BIRDS NEITHER SOW NOR REAP.` → `A RENT PAYMENT DUE.` → `SHOULD WE STOP SOWING?`

segments.voice: Day three hundred sixty-six met providence in Joseph's story; today, the Catechism's account. It starts somewhere surprising. Creation wasn't made finished. It was made on a journey, heading toward a fullness it hasn't reached yet, and providence is the name for the ways God guides it along that road. Scripture, the Catechism says, shows that care as concrete and close, reaching the smallest things. That's why Jesus asks for a child's kind of trust: "Seek ye therefore first the kingdom of God, and his justice, and all these things shall be added unto you." Then the turn. In the Catholic picture, God isn't a puppeteer. He gives his creatures not only existence but the dignity of acting on their own, of being real causes for each other. And to human beings he gives the power to share in providence freely: to tend the earth, to work, to look after one another. Writing about himself and the others who labored with him in Corinth, Paul says, in the Douay-Rheims, "we are God's coadjutors." Helpers, fellow workers. The Catechism takes up that phrase for people more broadly: through their actions, their prayers, and even their sufferings, people can enter freely into God's plan, and so become God's fellow workers. So, back to the birds. They don't sow. People do, and on this reading, the sowing itself can be part of how God provides. Providence isn't a reason to sit still, and it isn't a promise that nothing will go wrong. It's trust that God is at work, and an invitation to work alongside.
screen: `CREATION MADE ON A JOURNEY.` · `SEEK FIRST THE KINGDOM.` · `NOT A PUPPETEER: REAL CAUSES.` · `WE ARE GOD'S COADJUTORS.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you're carrying this week, a bill, a test result, a hard conversation, and ask two questions: what part of this is mine to do, and what part is out of my hands? Name your part, one step, nothing more, and let the other part go for now. If you pray, hand that part to God in your own words; if you don't, practice setting it down for these few minutes.
Providence. God's guidance of a creation still on its way, and the invitation to share in that work freely. Today's word.
Your line: we are co-workers. Care from above, and hands at work down here. Day one thousand seventy.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of trusting in divine providence, and pair that trust with work; some pray before a task or a decision and offer the day's work to God in a morning prayer.

chat.says: If God provides, why bother working so hard? Can't we just trust and wait?
options: The Catechism says God shares providence with us: our work and care can be part of how he provides.
Jesus told people to stop sowing, like the birds, so the Church tells people to quit their jobs.
Providence covers only the smallest things, like birds; the big things are left to chance.
chat.meaning: Creation is on a journey, and God guides it. The Catechism says God gives people the dignity of sharing in providence: Paul's word is coadjutors, fellow workers.

coadjutors.meaning: helpers, fellow workers: Paul's word in the Douay-Rheims

Sermon on the Mount.meaning: Jesus's hillside teaching in Matthew's Gospel

Corinth.meaning: a Greek city where Paul and others labored

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of Matthew 6:26, 6:33 and 1 Corinthians 3:9 ('For we are God's coadjutors').

Catechism paraphrased (copyright): creation 'in a state of journeying' (CCC 302); concrete and immediate care (CCC 303); childlike abandonment, citing Matthew 6:31–33 (CCC 305); the dignity of being causes (CCC 306); sharing in providence through actions, prayers and sufferings, as God's fellow workers (CCC 307). Confirm.
1 Corinthians 3:9: Paul is speaking of himself and Apollos; the script says so, and says the Catechism applies the phrase more broadly.
Hook: 'due on the first' is illustrative, not a claim.
